To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the subthalamic nuclei (STN) in the R6‐2 transgenic mouse of Huntington's disease exhibit altered activity in the low frequency band of the electrocorticogram (ECoG), which may contribute to the motor dysfunction seen in Huntington's disease (Huntington's Disease Society of America, 2012).
STN neuronal activity is altered and reduced in the R6 mouse model of Huntington’s disease, which may contribute to motor dysfunction.
the subthalamic nuclei (STN) are entrained to cortical low‐rate rhythms, and that this entrainment is disrupted in a mouse model of Huntington disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of neural activity in the subthalamic region of the brain in the pathophysiology of the Huntington disease (HD).
the role of the subthalamic (STN) nucleus in the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease and the mechanisms by which STN dysfunction leads to motor symptoms.
the relationship between cortical and subcortical oscillations and the role of these oscillations in the pathogenesis and treatment of HD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cortical‐STN neural entrainment is reduced in the R6 mouse model of HD and that this is a likely contributor to the motor symptoms observed in HD.
cortical entrainment to the subthalamic nuclei is disrupted in R2/6 mice and this may be one of many mechanisms contributing to the motor deficits in this disease model.
cortical entrainment to low frequencies of the STN is altered in HD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cortical low‐frequency rhythms entrain subthalamic neurons and such synchronization is reduced in R6/ 2 mice.
cortical‐subcortical synchrony is disrupted in the R6 mouse model of Huntington disease.
cortical‐STN synchrony is reduced in HD and this could lead to disordered motor function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the R6/ 2 transgenic mouse is an excellent model to study HD and that cortical entrainment is a critical mechanism that can be used to study the role of the basal ganglia in the pathogenesis of HD.

STN neurons are phase‐locked to low‐frequency oscillatory activity in the cortex and this entrainment is disrupted in the R6‐2 transgenic mouse of Huntington's disease, suggesting a potential mechanism for disordered motor control and cognitive deficits in HD patients.
the STN and cortex are less synchronized in HD mice and that this may be due to a reduction in low‐frequency cortical oscillations.
